lines: A few topics back, a per-file record of column metrics was read straight out of this format's metadata tree — a minimum value, a maximum value, a count of rows, treated as simple facts about the file.
Those facts aren't always as exact as they looked. Here's the part that got glossed over.

Picture a column holding a genuinely long piece of text, far longer than a typical identifier. That value gets written into a file, and this format still has to record a minimum and maximum for that column, in the metadata.
Does it store that long value in full, however long it happens to be? Or does it cut it down to a fixed length, at the cost of no longer being the literal value?
answer: It cuts it down. There's a fixed limit on how much of a text or binary value gets kept as a bound, and past that limit, what's stored stops being the literal minimum or maximum.
It becomes a safe range instead — close enough to rule out files during planning, but not a value anyone should trust as the literal smallest or largest thing in the column.

lines: That's exactly what happened here, with real values written by this chapter's own library. One value two hundred bytes long, another just over forty — both stored as bounds of exactly sixteen bytes.
The upper one isn't even a truncated copy of the real value. Its final byte is nudged up by one, specifically so it still sorts above the real value it's standing in for.

And that's not an implementation quirk, either. The specification says this outright: bounds on text and binary columns are never treated as exact, precisely because they might have been cut short when they were written.
A bound in this format's metadata is a safe range a planner can lean on to skip files. It was never a promise of the literal smallest or largest value.

So if per-file statistics are this limited — scattered across many small metadata records, each one potentially imprecise — where does a query planner actually get something like a real distinct-value count across an entire table?
Does it open every single file and count the exact values by hand, every time a query needs that number? Or does something else entirely handle it?
answer: Something else entirely. A separate kind of file exists specifically to hold statistics at the level of the whole table, not any one piece of it — including a compact, pre-built summary structure for estimating how many distinct values a column holds.
That summary isn't exact, and it isn't meant to be. It trades a small, known margin of error for never having to scan the table just to answer that one question.

lines: That exact kind of file was built here, for real, matching the file format's specification byte for byte — the right opening marker, the summary structure itself, and a closing section describing exactly what's inside and where to find it.

Inside it sits a real distinct-value-estimating structure, built from scratch in this sandbox, and the whole file was then registered against the table using this library's own genuine, public mechanism for attaching statistics — not a workaround, the real thing.

Then it was read back completely independently, parsing the raw bytes of that file by hand, because this particular library has no built-in way to read that summary structure back out once it's written.

The estimate that came out of it was checked directly against the table's actual, exactly-counted distinct value count. The two were close — not identical, which is exactly what a space-saving summary like this is supposed to produce.
One more file type worth naming here, though it wasn't built in this sandbox: the same whole-table statistics idea exists one level down, scoped to a single partition instead of the entire table.
It follows its own, separate specification, and just like the table-level version, a reader is free to simply ignore it if it isn't there.

Here's why any of this actually matters beyond being a nice-to-have. A real query engine's cost-based planner — the part deciding which order to perform joins in — leans directly on exactly these kinds of statistics to estimate which plan will be cheapest.

When those statistics are missing, or simply can't be computed, that engine falls back to a noticeably weaker planning strategy. And when the statistics are present but wrong, the risk isn't just a slightly worse plan — it's a genuinely bad one, built on a bad estimate.

So the full picture is this. Per-file statistics were already sitting in this format's metadata tree, but capped and sometimes truncated. A dedicated file type carries the whole-table picture instead, built and verified here from first principles.
The same idea repeats one level down, at the partition level. And none of it is decoration — a real query planner's choice of join order depends on these numbers being there, and being right.
